text:
This paper tackles sentence-level classification using convolutional neural networks built on top of pre-trained word vectors [P1_p1_c02]. Word vectors project sparse encodings onto a lower-dimensional space, serving as feature extractors that encode semantic features [P1_p1_c03]. 

The architecture begins with a sentence represented as $x_{1:n} = x_1 \oplus x_2 \oplus \dots \oplus x_n$, where $\oplus$ is the concatenation operator [P1_p2_c01]. A convolution operation applies a filter $w \in \mathbb{R}^{h \cdot k}$ to a window of $h$ words, generating a feature $c_i$ via $c_i = f(w \cdot x_{i:i+h-1} + b)$, where $b$ is a bias term and $f$ is a non-linear function like the hyperbolic tangent [P1_p2_c01]. This filter is applied to each word window to produce a feature map $c = [c_1, c_2, \dots, c_{n-h+1}]$ [P1_p2_c01]. Next, a max-over-time pooling operation takes the maximum value $\hat{c} = \max\{c\}$ as the feature, which naturally handles variable sentence lengths [P1_p2_c01]. Multiple filters with varying window sizes capture multiple features, passing through a fully connected layer with dropout and a softmax output [P1_p2_c01][P1_p2_c02]. The authors also propose a multichannel architecture where filters apply to both static and fine-tuned word vector channels, adding the results [P1_p1_c02][P1_p2_c02].

Experimentally, a simple CNN with static vectors achieves excellent results on multiple benchmarks, outperforming or competing with complex pooling and parse-tree methods [P1_p1_c02][P1_p4_c03]. Fine-tuning task-specific vectors yields further gains, and the models improve upon the state of the art on 4 out of 7 tasks, including sentiment analysis and question classification [P1_p1_c02][P1_p4_c03].
